name: Durga Puja in Siliguri and Jalpaiguri
when: Sep–Oct, five days ending on Dashami (lunar calendar)
summary: North Bengal's biggest festival. For five days Siliguri and Jalpaiguri fill with community pandals, lights, food stalls and crowds until late at night. It is also the busiest travel week of the year in the Dooars and the hills.
body: Durga Puja celebrates the goddess Durga's victory over the buffalo demon Mahishasura and her yearly return to her parents' home with her children. In Bengal it is as much a social and artistic festival as a religious one. UNESCO inscribed Durga Puja in Kolkata on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2021, and North Bengal's towns celebrate in the same spirit.

In Siliguri, neighbourhood clubs build hundreds of pandals, temporary structures of bamboo and cloth that range from traditional shrines to elaborate themed installations. Crowds go pandal-hopping from evening until the early hours, especially on Saptami, Ashtami and Navami, and food stalls sell everything from rolls and momos to sweets. Jalpaiguri, the old district town on the Teesta, has older family pujas alongside community ones.

On Dashami the images are taken in procession for immersion in the Mahananda and Teesta, and women play sindoor khela, smearing each other with vermilion. The next day, in many Rajbanshi communities of the Dooars, Bhandani Puja begins. For travellers, the key point is planning: trains, flights, hotels and safaris are booked out weeks ahead.
tips: Book trains, flights, rooms and Dooars safari slots as soon as booking opens if you plan to travel in Puja week.
Pandal-hop on foot or by toto after dark; roads near major pandals close to cars and traffic crawls.
If you want the Dooars quiet, travel the week after Puja instead; prices drop and the weather is clearer.

faqs.a: Durga Puja follows the lunar calendar and falls in September or October each year, over five main days from Shashthi to Dashami. Check the exact dates in a current Bengali calendar or puja listing before you travel, because they shift by a few weeks each year.

faqs.q: Is it a good idea to visit the Dooars during Durga Puja
faqs.a: Only if you book early and enjoy crowds. Puja week is the busiest of the year: rooms cost the most, safari slots sell out, and roads are slow. The upside is the festival atmosphere in Siliguri and Jalpaiguri. For calm wildlife viewing, come a week or two later.

faqs.q: Where are the best Durga Puja pandals in Siliguri
faqs.a: Large community pujas are spread across the city, especially in neighbourhoods off Hill Cart Road, Sevoke Road and around the main markets, and they change their themes every year. Ask locals or check local news for that year's popular pandals, and go late in the evening on Saptami to Navami.

On Dashami, the last day of Durga Puja, married women offer sindoor (vermilion) to the goddess before her immersion and then smear it on each other's faces and hair, wishing for good fortune. It is now often joined by women more widely. Ask before photographing participants.

name: Bhandani Puja
when: Oct, the day after Dashami (Ekadashi), lunar calendar
summary: A Rajbanshi festival of North Bengal held on Ekadashi, the day after Durga Puja ends, worshipping Devi Bhandani, a form of Durga who rides a tiger. The biggest gathering in Jalpaiguri district is at Barnish near Maynaguri, close to Lataguri.
body: Bhandani Puja is a century-old observance among the Rajbanshi community of North Bengal. It falls on Ekadashi, the day after Dashami, when the rest of Bengal has just said goodbye to Durga. One account told locally says that as the goddess left for Kailash after Dashami she was sad, and at the foot of the Himalaya the people of these plains worshipped her for one more day, after which she went home happy and blessed them. This is a story of faith, told in different ways.

Bhandani is shown with her children, like Durga, but her mount is a tiger rather than a lion. Village fairs grow up around the puja grounds with stalls, rides and food. In Jalpaiguri district the largest gathering is at Barnish in the Maynaguri block; Bhandani is also worshipped at Malbazar, Mekhliganj, Mathabhanga, Nagrakata, Khayerkata, Alipurduar, Ranirhat and other places.

For visitors staying at Lataguri over the Puja holidays, Barnish is a short drive away. Go in the afternoon, dress simply, and treat it as a local religious gathering rather than a show. Ask before photographing worshippers and the image, and be patient with crowds and traffic.
tips: If you are in Lataguri during the Puja week, plan the day after Dashami for a visit to Barnish near Maynaguri.
Carry small notes for fair stalls and offerings, and keep valuables secure in crowds.
Ask your lodge host which local Bhandani pujas are worth visiting that year; there are many small ones.

faqs.a: Bhandani Puja is a Rajbanshi festival of North Bengal held on Ekadashi, the day after Durga Puja ends. Devotees worship Devi Bhandani, a form of Durga whose mount is a tiger, along with her children. It is popular across the Dooars and Cooch Behar region.

In Jalpaiguri district the biggest gathering is at Barnish in the Maynaguri block, near Lataguri. It is also held at Malbazar, Mekhliganj, Mathabhanga, Nagrakata, Khayerkata, Alipurduar, Ranirhat and in many villages across the Dooars.

faqs.q: How is Bhandani different from Durga
faqs.a: Bhandani is regarded as a form of Durga worshipped by the Rajbanshi community the day after Dashami. Like Durga she is shown with her children, but she rides a tiger instead of a lion. Local accounts explain the extra day of worship in different ways.

Yes. The pujas and fairs are open public gatherings. Dress modestly, follow local customs at the shrine, ask before taking photographs, and be patient with crowds. Go in the afternoon or early evening, and return to your lodge before late night.

name: Karam Puja in the tea gardens
when: Aug–Sep, Ekadashi of the bright half of Bhado (lunar calendar)
summary: Karam is the harvest and fertility festival of Adivasi communities with roots in the Chota Nagpur plateau, and in the Dooars it is one of the great celebrations of the tea garden lines. A branch of the Karam tree is planted, worshipped and danced around through the night.
body: The Oraon, Munda and other communities whose ancestors came to the Dooars tea gardens from the Chota Nagpur plateau brought Karam with them. It falls on the eleventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of Bhado, in late August or September. Young women prepare by planting seeds of rice, wheat, maize and pulses in baskets, the jawa, and tending them for seven to nine days, often fasting.

On the festival day, people bring a branch of the Karam tree from the forest and plant it in the akhra, the village dance ground. It is washed with milk and rice beer and worshipped, the story of Karam is recited, and the community sings and dances around it to the beat of the mandar drum, often all night. The next day the branch is carried in procession and immersed in a river or pond.

In the Dooars, Karam falls in the monsoon, when the parks are closed and few tourists come. If you are in the region then, ask your host near Chalsa, Malbazar or Murti which garden lines are celebrating, and go only if invited or welcomed. It is a community festival, not a performance.
tips: Karam falls in the monsoon; plan for rain, flooded roads and closed parks.
Go with a local host who knows the community, and ask before photographing dancers or rituals.
Accept food or drink offered if you are comfortable, and leave before the late-night celebrations if you are not invited to stay.

faqs.a: Karam falls on the Ekadashi, the eleventh lunar day, of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhado, which comes in late August or September. Exact dates change each year with the lunar calendar. Check a current calendar or ask local contacts before you travel.

faqs.q: Who celebrates Karam in the Dooars
faqs.a: Mainly Adivasi communities such as the Oraon and Munda, whose ancestors came to work in the tea gardens from the Chota Nagpur plateau in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Karam is one of the biggest festivals in the tea garden lines of North Bengal.

Young women grow seedlings in baskets for about a week, a branch of the Karam tree is planted in the village dance ground and worshipped, the Karam story is told, and people sing and dance around it to the mandar drum, often all night. The branch is immersed in water the next day.

Sometimes, if you are welcomed by the community. Go with a local host, keep a low profile, ask before photographing, and do not treat it as a show. Since Karam falls in the monsoon, travel conditions in the Dooars can be difficult.

name: Jalpesh Mela at Shivaratri
summary: One of North Bengal's oldest and largest fairs, held at the Jalpesh Shiva temple near Maynaguri at Mahashivratri. It has been held since the seventeenth century and draws pilgrims and traders from across North Bengal, Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh.
body: The Jalpesh temple stands on the Jarda river about 7–8 km from Maynaguri, around 25 km from Lataguri. Building began in 1524 under the Koch ruler Bishwa Singha and the temple was rebuilt in 1563 and 1663. Its fair at Mahashivratri, in February or March, has run since the seventeenth century, and before independence elephants were traded here.

Today the mela fills the fields around the temple for several days with stalls of household goods, clothes, toys, sweets and food, rides for children and long queues of devotees waiting to offer water and bel leaves to the Shivalinga known as Anadi. Pilgrims come from all over North Bengal and from Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh. There is also a large pilgrimage in the month of Shravan, in July and August.

For visitors based at Lataguri in February or March, a morning at the Jalpesh Mela is a vivid contrast to the forest. Go early, before the crowds peak, keep your belongings close, and expect slow traffic on the Maynaguri road.
tips: Go early in the morning on a weekday of the fair to avoid the biggest crowds.
Leave valuables at your lodge and carry small notes for stalls and offerings.
Hire a car from Lataguri for the morning; buses and autos are packed during the mela.

faqs.a: The main Jalpesh Mela is held at Mahashivratri, which falls in February or March depending on the lunar calendar, and lasts several days. A second large pilgrimage happens in the month of Shravan, July–August. Check exact dates before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I reach the Jalpesh temple
faqs.a: The temple is about 7–8 km from Maynaguri town and roughly 25 km from Lataguri. Hire a car from Lataguri, or take a bus to Maynaguri and an auto or toto to the temple. During the mela, expect slow traffic and plan extra time.

faqs.q: How old is the Jalpesh fair
faqs.a: The Shivaratri fair at Jalpesh has been held since the seventeenth century, and the temple itself dates its first construction to 1524 under the Koch ruler Bishwa Singha. Before independence, elephants were traded at the fair.

faqs.q: Is the Jalpesh Mela safe for families
faqs.a: Generally yes, but it is very crowded. Keep children close and agree a meeting point, carry little cash, and avoid peak hours on the main Shivaratri day. Mornings on the days around Shivaratri are calmer.
